title: Rhoda at the door (Acts 12:1–17)
hook: Peter escapes prison, knocks, and the maid is so happy she forgets to open

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gentile, from the Latin for the nations: Peter walked into Cornelius's house.

This one starts dark. King Herod, a later Herod than the one in the Christmas story, has James, the brother of John, put to death with the sword. Seeing it pleases some people, he arrests Peter too, during Passover week, planning a public trial after the festival. Four squads of soldiers guard him. The night before the trial he's asleep between two of them, chained to both. Across the city, in the house of Mary, the mother of John Mark, the church is gathered, praying for him deep into the night. In the King James Bible: "prayer was made without ceasing of the church unto God for him." Hold on to that. They're praying for this.
screen: `JAMES IS KILLED.` → `PETER IN CHAINS.` → `PRAYER WITHOUT CEASING.`

segments.voice: In the prison, a light. An angel nudges Peter in the side: get up, quickly. The chains fall off his wrists. Put on your belt, the angel says, and your sandals. Now your cloak. Follow me. Peter follows, half asleep, sure he's dreaming: past the first guard, past the second, to the iron gate into the city, which opens by itself. They walk one street, and the angel is gone. Peter comes to himself: this is real. So he goes to Mary's house and knocks at the outer gate. A servant girl named Rhoda, which means rose, comes to answer. Here's Luke's line: "And when she knew Peter's voice, she opened not the gate for gladness, but ran in, and told how Peter stood before the gate." She's so happy she forgets to open the door. And the room full of people praying for Peter's release says, in the King James: "Thou art mad." She insists. Then it must be his angel, they say. Meanwhile, outside, a wanted man stands in the street: "But Peter continued knocking." When they open it, they're astonished. Two things to notice. Luke gives the servant girl a name: in a story full of kings, soldiers and apostles, the one who recognizes the voice is Rhoda, and she's remembered. And the church prayed hard, but when the answer came, it was standing on the doorstep, and they almost didn't let it in.
screen: `CHAINS FALL. FOLLOW ME.` · `SHE OPENED NOT THE GATE FOR GLADNESS.` · `THOU ART MAD.` · `BUT PETER CONTINUED KNOCKING.` · then, large: `ANSWERED PRAYERS KNOCK TOO.`

segments.voice: Look back over the last month for something good you'd hoped for that arrived, and that you nearly missed or didn't believe at first: a message left unread, good news you second-guessed, a kindness you assumed must be a mistake. Let yourself smile at it, or laugh, the way you'd laugh at Rhoda running in with the door still shut. If you pray, you can say thank you.
Rose. What the name Rhoda means, the servant girl so glad to hear Peter's voice at the door that she forgot to let him in.
Your line: answered prayers knock too. Tomorrow, a purple-cloth merchant, and singing at midnight. Day eighty-three, done.

howItsDone: Christians often tell the story of Rhoda with a smile, as a picture of praying hard and then being surprised by the answer. Catholics and others read Peter's escape on the feast of Saints Peter and Paul, June 29.

original.note: Greek: rose. The name of the servant girl who knew Peter's voice.

trapdoor: what you thought: a funny little scene with a maid.
what it means: the church prays all night for Peter's release, and when he's knocking at the door, they don't believe it.
what a scholar hears: Luke names a servant girl, Rhode, in a story of kings; the house belongs to Mary, mother of John Mark, a home where, Acts says, many were gathered praying.

notes: Herod here is Herod Agrippa I, grandson of Herod the Great; stated as 'a grandson of the Herod from the Christmas story'. Confirm.
Acts 12:1–11 is the first reading at the Mass of the day for Saints Peter and Paul (June 29) in the Roman lectionary; confirm, and confirm other churches that read it then.
'Passover week' renders 'the days of unleavened bread' (12:3–4). Confirm.
The script calls the author of Acts 'Luke', following church tradition; many scholars treat the authorship as uncertain. Confirm the traditional name is acceptable without a qualifier.
